question: How long is a statement on origin valid under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement?
expected: 12 months from the date it was made out, or longer if the importing Party provides so, up to a maximum of 24 months (Article 56(3)).
answer: Under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement, a statement on origin is valid for 12 months from the date it was made out, unless a Party decides to extend the period up to 24 months. This is specified in Article 56(3) of the Agreement [a7547bfef8-0022]. However, the UK has chosen to provide for a longer period of up to 24 months for imports into the UK of EU-origin goods [36b53d745c-0040]. The validity period applies to imports into the EU, where the EU is the importing Party, and is limited to 12 months [36b53d745c-0039]. The Commission does not provide information on third country policies, but the UK has extended the validity period for its own imports.

question: Under the EU-UK TCA, for how long must the exporter keep a copy of the statement on origin and the supporting records?
expected: At least four years after the statement on origin was made out (Article 59(2)); the importer keeps its records at least three years after importation.
answer: Under the EU-UK TCA, the exporter must keep a copy of the statement on origin and the supporting records for a minimum of four years after the date the statement on origin was made out [a7547bfef8-0026]. This requirement applies to both the statement on origin and all other records demonstrating that the product satisfies the requirements to obtain originating status. The records may be kept in electronic format as permitted.

question: What is the general tolerance for non-originating materials in the EU-UK TCA for products outside Chapters 50 to 63?
expected: 10 % of the ex-works price of the product (Article 42(1)(b)); textiles follow Notes 7 and 8 of Annex 2.
answer: The general tolerance for non-originating materials in the EU-UK TCA for products outside Chapters 50 to 63 is 10% of the ex-works price of the product. This is specified in Article 42 of the TCA [a7547bfef8-0006]. The tolerance allows up to 10% of non-originating materials, but it cannot exceed the limit set by the product-specific rules [a7547bfef8-0006].

question: Under the EU-UK TCA, up to what value are small packages and travellers' personal luggage imported into the EU exempt from a statement on origin?
expected: EUR 500 for small packages and EUR 1 200 for personal luggage (Article 60(2)(b)(ii)); the UK sets its own limits.
answer: Under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA), small consignments and travellers' personal luggage imported into the EU are exempt from the requirement for a statement on origin if their total value does not exceed EUR 500 for products sent in small packages from a private person to a private person, or EUR 1,200 for products in travellers' personal luggage [4af5af7293-0015]. This exemption applies to goods that are not of commercial nature and are not imported by way of trade. However, the exemption does not relieve traders from the responsibility of ensuring that the goods are originating in the EU or the UK to benefit from zero duty treatment. If the importing authorities have doubts about the declaration, duties may apply.

question: UK customs is verifying our customer's preference claim and has asked the EU customs authorities for information about our goods. If 10 months pass without an answer from the EU side, what can happen?
expected: UK customs may deny preferential tariff treatment: Article 63(1)(c) allows it when, within 10 months of the request under Article 62(2), the exporting Party's customs authority has not replied or its reply does not confirm origin.
answer: If 10 months pass without an answer from the EU side, the UK customs authority may deny preferential tariff treatment, as outlined in Article 63 of the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement. This denial could occur if the EU customs authority does not provide the required information or if the information provided is inadequate to confirm the product's origin. The EU has a transitional period for exporters to make statements on origin, but if this period has expired and no statement has been provided, the UK customs authority may deny the preferential treatment. [36b53d745c-0059]

question: Does the EU-UK TCA prohibit duty drawback on non-originating materials?
expected: No. It only provides that, not earlier than two years after entry into force and at the request of either Party, the Trade Specialised Committee shall review the Parties' duty drawback and inward-processing schemes (Article 53): the review is mandatory once a Party asks for it.
answer: The EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) allows duty drawback on non-originating materials [3804f88053-0280]. This is because there is no prohibition of duty drawback in the EU-UK TCA, as stated in the guidance. The TCA permits duty drawback for non-originating materials, which means that imported non-originating materials can be used in the production of goods exported under the TCA, and the duties on these materials can be refunded.

question: We sell a gift set to the UK made of EU-originating products plus one item bought from China. Can the whole set still count as originating under the TCA?
expected: Yes, if the value of the non-originating components does not exceed 15 % of the ex-works price of the set (Article 48).
answer:
The gift set consists of EU-originating products and one item from China. Under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA), a set is considered originating if all its components are originating, or if the value of non-originating components does not exceed 15% of the ex-works price of the set. Since the non-originating item (from China) has a value that exceeds 15% of the set's ex-works price, the entire set cannot be considered originating under the TCA. 

This is based on the guidance provided in [a7547bfef8-0013] and [4af5af7293-0001], which state that a set is considered originating only if all components are originating or if the value of non-originating components does not exceed 15% of the set's value.

question: We export plug-in hybrid and fully electric cars from the EU to the UK this year. What product-specific rule of origin do they have to meet under the TCA?
expected: MaxNOM 55 % (EXW): non-originating materials may not exceed 55 % of the ex-works price. This interim rule of Annex 5, Section 2 applies from 1 January 2024 until 31 December 2026; until the end of 2023 it was MaxNOM 60 %.
answer:
The EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) specifies that for vehicles equipped with an internal combustion engine, the value of non-originating materials may not exceed 45% of the ex-works price of the finished product. If the UK and/or European parts account for at least 55% of the final value, no customs duty applies when vehicles are exported to the EU [36b53d745c-0145]. For plug-in hybrid and electric cars, the rule requires that battery blocks of heading 85.07 be originating, and for the first 6 years of the agreement, more flexible rules apply [36b53d745c-0145]. 

If an EU spirit is shipped to the UK for an ageing process and then returned to the EU without acquiring a UK preferential origin, it may still retain its EU origin under the TCA, provided the ageing process meets the conditions for bilateral cumulation of origin [36b53d745c-0088]. 

For plug-in hybrids and electric cars, the product-specific rule of origin is MaxNOM 55% (EXW) for plug-in hybrids and MaxNOM 60% (EXW) for electric cars [d31784ed8e-0001].

question: We assemble EV battery packs in the EU from battery cells imported from Asia and sell them to the UK. Is the assembly enough for the packs to be EU originating under the TCA?
expected: No, assembly alone is no longer enough. Until 31 December 2026 the battery packs of 85.07 need a change of tariff heading, except from non-originating active cathode materials, or non-originating materials not exceeding 40 % of the ex-works price (Annex 5, Section 2). Assembling packs from non-originating cells only qualified until the end of 2023.
answer:
Under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement, the transitional product-specific rules for electric accumulators and electrified vehicles apply until 31 December 2023. For battery packs used in vehicles under headings 87.02–87.04, the rule requires that the battery cells or modules must be sourced from the EU or meet a MaxNOM of 70% (EXW) from non-originating materials. If the assembly occurs in the EU, it may qualify as EU originating under the transitional rules [d31784ed8e-0000]. 

From 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2026, the rules change to require that battery cells or modules must be sourced from the EU or meet a MaxNOM of 40% or 50% from non-originating materials, depending on the product [d31784ed8e-0002]. 

If an EU spirit is shipped to the UK for an ageing process without any additions or alterations, it may still retain EU origin under the TCA, provided it meets the conditions for bilateral cumulation of origin [36b53d745c-0088]. 

For EV battery packs assembled in the EU from Asian battery cells, the assembly itself may be sufficient to qualify as EU originating under the transitional rules, provided the materials meet the required MaxNOM thresholds [d31784ed8e-0000]. 

If you are exporting EV battery packs to the UK, ensure that the materials meet the applicable MaxNOM requirements to claim EU origin under the TCA.

question: For how long is a long-term supplier's declaration normally valid under the EU-UK TCA?
expected: Up to two years from the date it is made out; customs may allow longer periods (Annex 6, point 3).
answer: The long-term supplier’s declaration under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement is normally valid for a period of up to two years from the date of making out the declaration [36b53d745c-0022]. The customs authorities of the Party where the declaration is made may allow longer periods under certain conditions. The declaration must be made in the form provided for in Appendix 6-B and must describe the products in sufficient detail to enable them to be identified [ec6d601777-0003].

question: Which code goes in the EU customs declaration when a TCA preference claim is based on a statement on origin, and which one when it is based on importer's knowledge?
expected: U116 for a statement on origin, U117 for importer's knowledge, U118 for a statement covering multiple shipments of identical products.
answer: When a TCA preference claim is based on a statement on origin, the code to be used in the EU customs declaration is U116 [4af5af7293-0012]. When the claim is based on importer’s knowledge, the code to be used is U117 [4af5af7293-0012]. The code U118 is used for statements on origin for multiple shipments of identical products [4af5af7293-0012].

question: If an importer did not claim preference when importing goods under the EU-UK TCA, how long do they have to claim it retrospectively?
expected: Up to three years after the importation, on the basis of a statement on origin or of the importer's knowledge.
answer: If an importer did not claim preference when importing goods under the EU-UK TCA, they have up to three years after the date of importation to claim it retrospectively [36b53d745c-0059]. This period is extended to 2021 for supplier declarations, but the three-year rule applies generally for retrospective claims. The importer can claim preference based on a statement on origin or their own knowledge, with different codes (U116 or U117) used in the customs declaration depending on the basis of the claim [4af5af7293-0012]. The three-year period is the key rule for retrospective claims under the EU-UK TCA.

question: Can EU goods sent to a distribution centre in the UK and then re-exported to the EU without processing benefit from preferential treatment?
expected: No: they have not obtained UK originating status. Transit or returned goods procedures may avoid the tariffs.
answer:
EU goods sent to a distribution centre in the UK and then re-exported to the EU without processing may benefit from preferential treatment under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) if they meet the requirements of the Product Specific Rule (PSR) for the product. However, if the goods are not originating from the UK, they do not automatically qualify for preferential treatment in the EU. The UK's withdrawal from the Single Market and Customs Union means that goods imported from the UK are subject to customs formalities and may incur tariffs. 

This applies to goods that are non-originating (non-EU or UK) and are imported into the UK and then re-exported to the EU without processing. The TCA allows for duty drawbacks (DDBs) if the processing meets the requirements of the PSR. 

If the goods are re-exported to the EU under the TCA, they can benefit from preferential treatment if the processing meets the PSR requirements. However, if the goods are not originating from the UK, they do not automatically qualify for preferential treatment in the EU. 

The UK's customs procedures and the PSR requirements must be considered to determine if preferential treatment applies.

question: Does a statement on origin under the EU-UK TCA have to be signed?
expected: No, a signature is not required.
answer:
Under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA), a signature is not required in the declaration of origin for the purposes of the TCA [36b53d745c-0037]. The statement on origin can be made out on an invoice or any other document that describes the product in sufficient detail to identify it. The exporter is responsible for ensuring the information provided in the statement is correct and accurate [4af5af7293-0006]. 

If the UK customer cannot register for REX, the EU supplier can still issue a statement on origin if they are registered in REX for consignments of more than EUR 6000 [36b53d745c-0016]. The EU supplier is responsible for fulfilling the conditions of the origin chapter of the TCA. 

The TCA does not require a signature for the declaration of origin, and the statement can be made out on any document that adequately describes the product.

question: May a TCA statement on origin indicate the origin with abbreviations such as EU, UE, UK or GB?
expected: Yes, in full or abbreviated; statements made out in the EU should not name individual Member States.
answer:
The TCA allows the origin of products to be indicated either in full or using abbreviations. For the EU, the origin may be indicated as "the Union," "European Union," "EU," or "UE." For the UK, the origin may be indicated as "the United Kingdom," "UK," or "GB." Abbreviations like "EU" or "UE" are acceptable for the EU, but "UK" or "GB" are acceptable for the UK. The use of abbreviations is limited to the respective regions, and "GB" covers the entire United Kingdom, including Northern Ireland. 

[36b53d745c-0042][3804f88053-0196]

question: Do UK exporters need an EU REX number to make out statements on origin under the TCA?
expected: No. They use the reference number assigned under UK rules (the GB EORI number); the UK does not use REX.
answer:
The statement on origin for a UK exporter must include a reference number by which the exporter is identified, which is assigned according to the UK rules, specifically the GB EORI number. For EU exporters, the REX number is required for consignments exceeding EUR 6,000, but for consignments of less than EUR 6,000, no REX registration is required. UK exporters must include a GB EORI number in the statement on origin regardless of the consignment value. The EU-UK TCA does not require EU exporters to include an EORI number on the invoice, but they must include their REX number in the statement on origin for consignments over EUR 6,000. The REX system is used by EU exporters to verify their eligibility for preferential treatment under the TCA. 

[36b53d745c-0003][4af5af7293-0010]

question: Which annex of the EU-UK TCA contains the text of the statement on origin, and is it the same as Annex ORIG-4?
expected: Annex 7. Annex ORIG-4 is the earlier numbering of the same annex, still used in the Commission's Q&A; the guide for traders writes 'Annex 7 TCA (ex-Annex ORIG-4)'.
answer: The text of the statement on origin is contained in Annex ORIG-4 of the EU-UK TCA [36b53d745c-0037]. This annex specifies that the statement on origin can be made out on an invoice or any other document that describes the originating product in sufficient detail to identify it. The answer is based on the information provided in the passage [36b53d745c-0037].

question: Under the EU-Japan EPA, up to what value are small packages imported into Japan admitted as originating without a statement on origin?
expected: 100,000 yen, or such amount as Japan may establish (Article 3.20(2)(b)); for the EU, EUR 500 and EUR 1,200.
answer:
Under the EU-Japan EPA, small packages imported into Japan are admitted as originating without a statement on origin provided they meet the following criteria:  
1. The total value of the products does not exceed 500 euros for small packages or 1,200 euros for products forming part of travellers' personal luggage [a5f860bda7-0025].  
2. The products are not imported by way of trade and have been declared as satisfying the requirements of this Chapter.  
3. There is no doubt as to the veracity of such a declaration.  

The amounts are converted to the equivalent in the Member State's currency as at the first working day of October of each year, with the European Central Bank's published amounts applying from 1 January of the following year [a5f860bda7-0025].

question: What is the general tolerance for non-originating materials in the EU-Japan EPA?
expected: 10 % of the ex-works or free on board price of the product, for Chapters 1-49 and 64-97 (Article 3.6); textiles follow Notes 6 to 8 of Annex 3-A.
answer: The general tolerance for non-originating materials in the EU-Japan EPA is 10% of the ex-works or free on board (FOB) price of the product, as stated in Article 3.6 of the EU-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement [a5f860bda7-0008]. This applies to products classified under Chapters 1 to 49 or Chapters 64 to 97 of the Harmonized System. The tolerance is based on the ex-works price, and the EU-Japan EPA allows either ex-works or FOB prices to be used for calculations [3804f88053-0048].

question: Which origin criterion code must the exporter indicate on an EU-Japan statement on origin when the product is originating thanks to the tolerance?
expected: Code "E" (tolerance referred to in Article 3.6).
answer: The exporter must indicate the origin criterion code "2" on an EU-Japan statement on origin when the product is originating due to a maximum value of non-originating materials or a minimum regional value content rule. This is specified in Annex 3-D of the EU-Japan EPA Guidance [4c45e9934a-0003].

question: Does a statement on origin under the EU-Japan EPA need a signature or a stamp?
expected: No, it does not need to be signed or stamped by the exporter or by any governmental authority.
answer: A statement on origin under the EU-Japan EPA does not need a signature or a stamp. The passage explicitly states that "A statement on origin does not need to be signed or stamped by the exporter or by any governmental authority" [4c45e9934a-0017].

question: Which reference number identifies a Japanese exporter on an EU-Japan statement on origin?
expected: The Japan Corporate Number.
answer: The reference number that identifies a Japanese exporter on an EU-Japan statement on origin is the Japan Corporate Number [4c45e9934a-0009]. This number is assigned by the National Tax Agency in Japan and is used to identify the exporter in the statement. If no number is assigned, the exporter may indicate their full address under the "Place and date" section [4c45e9934a-0009].

question: Under the EU-Japan EPA, what rule applies to cars of heading 87.03 from the seventh year after entry into force?
expected: MaxNOM 45 % (EXW) or RVC 60 % (FOB) (Appendix 3-B-1, Section 2); before it was 55/50 and 50/55.
answer:
Under the EU-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement, for cars of heading 87.03, the rule applicable from the seventh year after entry into force is MaxNOM 45 % (EXW); or RVC 60 % (FOB). This is specified in Section 2 of Appendix 3-B-1, paragraph 3, which outlines the interim threshold for vehicles. The rule applies to products directly exported from a Party to the other Party and does not apply to products incorporated into a complete vehicle as materials in the exporting Party. 

[0a83c985d6-0001] [0a83c985d6-0005]

question: A French winegrower uses bentonite imported from the US to clarify wine exported to Japan. Does the bentonite prevent the wine from being wholly obtained?
expected: No. It is filtered out and not present in the final product, so it is a neutral element (Article 3.13 of the EU-Japan EPA) and criterion A can be indicated.
answer: According to the EU-Japan EPA guidance, bentonite used in the production of wine is considered a neutral element because it is filtered out at the end of the process and not present in the final product [3804f88053-0262]. This means that the bentonite does not need to be taken into account when determining whether the wine was wholly obtained in the EU. Therefore, the wine exported to Japan would be considered as wholly obtained in the EU, and the origin criterion “A” can be indicated on the statement on origin.

question: Under the EU-Korea FTA, up to what value can any exporter (not an approved exporter) make out an origin declaration?
expected: For consignments whose total value does not exceed 6000 euros (Article 16(1)(b)); above that, only approved exporters.
answer: Under the EU-Korea FTA, any exporter (not an approved exporter) can make an origin declaration if the total value of the consignment of originating products does not exceed 6000 euros [89c49ea6e4-0021]. This applies to both types of declarations (invoice or origin declaration) as long as the products are exported or exported and presented in the importing Party no longer than two years or the period specified in the importing Party's legislation after importation [89c49ea6e4-0022].

question: For how long must the exporter keep a copy of the origin declaration under the EU-Korea FTA?
expected: Five years (Article 23(1)).
answer: Under the EU-Korea FTA, the exporter must keep a copy of the origin declaration for five years, as stated in Article 23 of the Protocol on origin [89c49ea6e4-0030]. This includes the origin declaration and the documents referred to in Article 16.3. The records may also include electronic records.

question: What is the value limit for small packages imported into Korea without a proof of origin?
expected: 1000 US dollars, for small packages and for travellers' personal luggage alike (Article 21(3)(b)).
answer: The value limit for small packages imported into Korea without a proof of origin is 1000 US dollars. This is specified in Article 21, paragraph 3(a) of the EU-Korea Free Trade Agreement Protocol [89c49ea6e4-0027].

question: How must a handwritten origin declaration be written under the EU-Korea FTA?
expected: In ink, in capital characters (Article 16(4)).
answer: A handwritten origin declaration under the EU-Korea FTA must be written in ink in capital characters [89c49ea6e4-0022]. The declaration must include the exporter's signature in addition to the name of the person signing the declaration, and it must be in the linguistic version specified in Annex III of the origin protocol [bae57b2b4f-0003]. The text of the origin declaration appears in Annex III, and the declaration must be made out on an invoice, delivery note, or other commercial document.

question: Korean customs doubts our origin declaration and has sent a verification request to the EU customs authorities. What happens to our customer's preference if no answer arrives within 10 months?
expected: Korean customs shall, except in exceptional circumstances, refuse the preference; the same applies if the reply is not sufficient to determine the authenticity of the declaration or the real origin of the products (Article 27(7)).
answer: If no answer arrives within 10 months of the verification request, the EU customs authorities may refuse entitlement to the preference [7]. This applies in cases of reasonable doubt and does not require exceptional circumstances. The verification request must include findings and facts, and the results must clearly indicate whether the documents are authentic and whether the products are originating in a Party and fulfill the other requirements of the Protocol. If no reply is received within 10 months, the EU customs authorities may refuse the preference.

question: Can an origin declaration under the EU-Korea FTA be made out after the goods have been exported?
expected: Yes, if it is presented in the importing Party no longer than two years (or the period in its legislation) after the importation (Article 16(6)).
answer: Under the EU-Korea FTA, an origin declaration may be made out after the goods have been exported, provided that the declaration is presented in the importing Party no longer than two years or the period specified in the legislation of the importing Party after the importation of the products [89c49ea6e4-0022]. The declaration must be made out by the exporter and must be in accordance with the legislation of the exporting Party [89c49ea6e4-0022].

question: How long is an origin declaration valid under CETA?
expected: 12 months from the date it was completed by the exporter, or longer if the Party of import provides so (Article 20).
answer: An origin declaration under CETA is valid for 12 months from the date it was completed by the exporter [dc1e68a1fd-0033]. If the declaration is completed for multiple shipments, the period of validity must not exceed 12 months, and all importations must occur within that period [dc1e68a1fd-0033]. The Party of import may accept the declaration after the validity period for the purpose of preferential tariff treatment [dc1e68a1fd-0033].

question: Under CETA, for how long must the exporter keep the origin declaration and supporting documents?
expected: Three years after completing the origin declaration, or longer if the Party of export specifies (Article 26(1)).
answer: Under CETA, the exporter must keep the origin declaration and supporting documents for three years after the completion of the origin declaration, as specified in Article 26, paragraph 1 [dc1e68a1fd-0040]. If the exporter based the origin declaration on a written statement from the producer, the producer must maintain records in accordance with paragraph 1 [dc1e68a1fd-0040].

question: What is the general tolerance for non-originating materials under CETA?
expected: 10 % of the transaction value or ex-works price of the product (Article 6(1)(a)).
answer:
The general tolerance for non-originating materials under CETA is up to 10 per cent of the transaction value or ex-works price of the product, as stated in Article 6(a) of the Protocol on rules of origin [dc1e68a1fd-0011]. This tolerance allows the use of non-originating materials where the list rule would not permit it, provided the conditions in Annex 5 are met. 

The general tolerance applies to all products, including textile and apparel products, and is subject to the requirements of the Protocol [dc1e68a1fd-0011]. 

The general tolerance is also explained in the European Commission's Guidance on preferential rules of origin, which states that it allows the use of non-originating materials up to a specific percentage of the ex-works price or weight of the final product [3804f88053-0049]. 

The general tolerance is not limited to textiles and is applicable to all products covered by the agreement.

question: We are a Canadian garment maker that sews shirts from fabric imported from China. Can the shirts be exported to the EU as originating under CETA?
expected: As a rule, no: CETA textiles and apparel follow double transformation, so sewing imported fabric is not enough. The exception is the limited, reciprocal origin quotas by product category (Annex 6), whose volumes are not in the corpus.
answer:
The Canadian garment maker can export shirts to the EU as originating under CETA, provided the fabric is imported from China under inward processing and the shirts are made in the EU. The EU-Canada CETA prohibits duty drawback for cotton fabric, but this rule does not apply to garments. The shirts are made from fabric that is imported from China under inward processing, so the fabric is considered originating in the EU. The EU-Canada CETA requires that the fabric is "cut and attached to originating soles" in the EU to qualify as originating. Since the shirts are made in the EU and meet the requirements, they are considered originating under CETA. 

[3804f88053-0280]

question: Under the EU-Mercosur interim agreement, for how long must the exporter keep the statement on origin?
expected: At least 3 years from the date it was made out; the importer, at least 3 years from importation (Article 3.22).
answer: The exporter must keep the statement on origin for at least 3 years as of the date of making out the statement on origin [13fbe87e43-0027]. The importer must keep the statement on origin, or a copy thereof, for at least 3 years as of the date of importation of the products to which that statement on origin refers [13fbe87e43-0027].

question: Will the EU accept a 'certificate of origin' issued in a Mercosur country under the interim agreement, and for how long?
expected: Yes, as a transitional measure, for up to 3 years from entry into force, extendable by up to 2 years by notification (Annex 3-D).
answer: The EU accepts a 'certificate of origin' issued in a Mercosur country under the EU-Mercosur Interim Agreement on Trade, provided it meets the requirements set out in Annex 3-D ITA [04c8b496fb-0060]. This certificate is valid for a maximum period of five years from the date of entry into force of the agreement [638fb4ef97-0005]. The certificate may be issued in English, Portuguese, or Spanish by authorized entities in Mercosur and must be completed in full, with the exception of optional boxes 5 and 12 [04c8b496fb-0019]. The EU was informed of the choice made by each Mercosur signatory state regarding the use of the certificate as a statement on origin, up to five years from the provisional application of the agreement [04c8b496fb-0060].

question: Does the EU-Mercosur interim agreement prohibit duty drawback?
expected: No. It has no drawback prohibition, so materials under inward processing can keep duties suspended when originating products are exported to Mercosur.
answer: The EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement (ITA) does not prohibit duty drawback [04c8b496fb-0042]. If non-originating materials are used in the manufacture of a product in the EU, those materials are eligible for duty drawback when the products acquire EU preferential origin. This applies mainly to products under the inward processing procedure in the EU. Therefore, the suspended duty does not need to be paid when the materials used to manufacture an originating product are exported to Mercosur.

question: Which reference number must Argentinian exporters show on a statement on origin under the EU-Mercosur agreement?
expected: Their CUIT (Clave única de identificación tributaria), an 11-digit tax number, whatever the value of the shipment, plus name and signature.
answer: Argentinian exporters under the EU-Mercosur agreement must include their Single Tax Identification Number (CUIT) as a reference number on a statement on origin [04c8b496fb-0014]. The CUIT is a 11-digit number, such as 12345678901 or 20-00000000-3. This number is required regardless of the value of the originating products in the shipment. Additionally, the statement must include the exporter's name and a handwritten, electronic, or digital signature [04c8b496fb-0014].

question: From what date has the EU-Mercosur interim trade agreement been provisionally applied?
expected: From 1 May 2026.
answer: The EU-Mercosur Interim Trade Agreement (ITA) has been provisionally applied from 1 May 2026 [04c8b496fb-0002].

question: Can a Paraguayan exporter use the Annex 3-C statement on origin to obtain preferential treatment in the EU?
expected: No: for the time being Paraguay uses only the statement on origin in the form of a 'certificate' under Annex 3-D.
answer: A Paraguayan exporter cannot use the Annex 3-C statement on origin to obtain preferential treatment in the EU, as Paraguay has chosen to use only the "certificate" under Annex 3-D ITA for the transitional period. This means that during the five-year transition period, Paraguay can only use the "certificate" under Annex 3-D ITA. [638fb4ef97-0003][638fb4ef97-0002]

question: Which supporting document code is declared in the EU for a statement on origin under the EU-Mercosur agreement?
expected: U126 (with preference code 300, or 320 for quotas).
answer: The supporting document code declared in the EU for a statement on origin under the EU-Mercosur agreement is U126 Statement on origin [04c8b496fb-0004]. This code is specified in the D.E. type of supporting document 12 03 002 000, which outlines the requirements for statements on origin.

question: How long is a proof of origin valid under the revised PEM Convention?
expected: Ten months from the date of issue or making out in the exporting Contracting Party (Article 23).
answer: Under the revised PEM Convention, a proof of origin is valid for ten months from the date of issue or making out in the exporting Contracting Party. question: What is the value tolerance for non-originating materials under the revised PEM rules for industrial products?

answer: Under the revised PEM rules, the value tolerance for non-originating materials is 10% of the ex-works price of the product, as stated in the guidance [3804f88053-0057]. This applies to products other than those covered by point (a) of Article 5. For industrial products, the 15% tolerance applies to the net weight of the product, but the value tolerance is 10% of the ex-works price [3804f88053-0057].

question: Does the revised PEM Convention prohibit duty drawback?
expected: Only for non-originating materials used in products of Chapters 50 to 63 (textiles), with exceptions for certain cumulation and bilateral trade (Article 16).
answer: The revised PEM Convention prohibits duty drawback for non-originating materials used in the manufacture of products falling within Chapters 50 to 63 of the Harmonised System, provided a proof of origin is issued or made out in accordance with Title V of this Appendix [706bb77c4a-0028]. The prohibition applies to any arrangement for refund, remission, or non-payment of customs duties or charges having an equivalent effect, applicable in the exporting Contracting Party to materials used in the manufacture, where such refund, remission, or non-payment applies when products obtained from the said materials are exported [706bb77c4a-0028]. The exporter must submit documents proving that no drawback has been obtained in respect of the non-originating materials used in the manufacture of the products concerned and that all customs duties or charges having equivalent effect applicable to such materials have actually been paid upon request from the customs authorities [706bb77c4a-0028]. The prohibition of duty drawback applies from 21 September 2020 [3804f88053-0284].

question: Which proofs of origin does the revised PEM Convention provide for?
expected: The movement certificate EUR.1 and the origin declaration on an invoice or other commercial document (Article 17); parties may agree on statements by registered exporters.
answer:
The revised PEM Convention provides for two types of proofs of origin:  
1. A movement certificate EUR.1, as specified in Annex IV of the Appendix [706bb77c4a-0055].  
2. An origin declaration, which can be provided by the exporter on an invoice, delivery note, or other commercial document, as outlined in Article 17 [706bb77c4a-0055].  

These proofs are required for products originating in one of the Contracting Parties when imported into another Contracting Party.

question: We export the same machines from Spain to Switzerland under the revised PEM rules and to Korea. Our importers sometimes clear the goods 11 months after we make out the proof of origin. Is it still valid in each market?
expected: In Korea, yes: a proof of origin is valid for 12 months (Article 18). Under the PEM rules, no: validity is ten months (Article 23); a late proof may only be accepted in exceptional circumstances or if the goods were presented to customs before the deadline.
answer: Under the revised PEM rules, a proof of origin is valid for ten months from the date of issue or making out in the exporting Contracting Party [706bb77c4a-0040]. If the importer clears the goods 11 months after the proof of origin is made out, this exceeds the ten-month validity period, but the customs authorities of the importing Contracting Party may accept the proof of origin if the delay is due to exceptional circumstances [706bb77c4a-0040]. In the case of Korea, the customs authorities may accept the proof of origin if the products were presented to customs before the final date [706bb77c4a-0040]. For Switzerland, the same applies, as the validity period is ten months from the date of issue. Therefore, the proof of origin may still be accepted in both markets, provided the delay is due to exceptional circumstances.

question: When is a pick-up type multipurpose vehicle classified in heading 8704 instead of 8703?

question: Where are motorised ploughs classified when the plough is permanently attached to a chassis with an engine?

question: ¿Caduca el número REX de un exportador registrado?
expected: No, su validez no está limitada en el tiempo, salvo revocación.
answer: El número REX de un exportador registrado no está limitado en el tiempo [3ac8ead017-0022]. Si se revoca el registro, las autoridades competentes establecen una fecha a partir de la cual la revocación surtirá efecto, limitando así la validez del número REX hasta esa fecha [3ac8ead017-0022]. La validez del número REX se mantiene hasta que se revoca el registro o se cumpla con los requisitos para su revocación.

question: ¿Qué estructura tiene un número REX?
expected: Código ISO del país (2 letras), «REX» (3 letras) y una cadena de hasta 30 caracteres alfanuméricos.
answer: El número REX tiene una estructura específica que incluye un identificador único asignado al exportador registrado. Este número se utiliza para certificar el origen de las mercancías exportadas en el contexto de acuerdos comerciales preferenciales [3ac8ead017-0006]. El número REX no está limitado en el tiempo y se puede utilizar en todos los acuerdos comerciales preferenciales en los que el sistema de certificación de origen aplicado sea el sistema REX [3ac8ead017-0022]. La validez del número REX no se limita a un período específico [3ac8ead017-0022].

question: Si me revocan el registro REX y vuelvo a registrarme, ¿recupero mi antiguo número?
expected: No: se asigna un número nuevo y no se reutiliza el revocado, salvo que la revocación se anule.
answer:
Si me revocan el registro REX y vuelvo a registrarme, el antiguo número de registro no se reutilizará [6]. Las autoridades competentes asignarán un nuevo número de registro al exportador y no reutilizarán el antiguo número de registro revocado, excepto en el caso de anulación de la revocación [6]. 

La validez del número de registro no está limitada en el tiempo, pero la revocación implica que el número de registro pierde su validez y no se puede utilizar para nuevos registros [3ac8ead017-0022]. 

En la UE, el número de registro revocado no debe utilizarse para nuevos registros de exportadores [3ac8ead017-0025]. 

La revocación se solicita desde el portal REX Trader, y el nuevo registro se registrará con un número diferente al anterior [3ac8ead017-0025]. 

Por lo tanto, no se recupera el antiguo número de registro revocado.
